newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti waits for new prime minister, U.N. decision.
newsitem.headline: Haiti waits for new prime minister, U.N. decision.

text.p: Haiti, its economy at a standstill, is gripped by uncertainty as the prime minister's office lies vacant and a decision nears on whether U.N. troops will leave at the end of this month.

"The country is at a standstill right now," said Chamber of Commerce President Fritz Kinol, who issued a study this week saying trade is at an all-time low. "There is an expectation of something new and no one knows if it will be good."
More than a month after Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resigned in the face of popular opposition to privatisation plans, President Rene Preval has not named a replacement.
"These days everyone is more interested to know when a prime minister will finally be named than who will be named," a columnist wrote in the Haitian daily Le Nouvelliste.

Political leaders, even from within the Lavalas political coalition that brought Preval to power, have been demanding he make a choice immediately. "Preval is refusing to carry out his responsibilities to name a new prime minister," the Open Gate Party, part of Lavalas, said in a statement this week.

Kinol and other economic officials said Eric Pierre, Haiti's representative on the Inter-American Development Bank's board of directors, was the most likely candidate. Pierre declined to comment on his possible nomination or on the Haitian economic situation when contacted by Reuters.

As an IADB official who has worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development and the U.S. Embassy in Haiti, Pierre would likely be a target for anti-privatisation popular organisations who forced Smarth's resignation. These groups called general strikes and demonstrations that sometimes turned into violent rock-throwing melees.

Preval said this week he will not back down from the plan to privatise nine state enterprises such as the telephone and electricity companies. "Where are we today?" he asked. "Teleco cannot provide phone lines, the electricity company doesn't provide electricity. We have to modernise, bring in capital and improve services."

Preval hopes to bring private investment and technology to Haiti through joint ventures, management contracts and concessions. Hundreds of millions of dollars in loans and grants from international monetary institutions like the IADB and World Bank are tied to the privatisation plan.

"The sector opposed to modernisation will see Pierre as a creature of the World Bank, of the IMF, as coming from Washington, D.C.," Kinol said. "The issue is not the capacity of the person but their political profile."

The popular groups, called collectively However it Falls it Falls, voiced growing anti-foreigner sentiment this week, demanding Parliament charge Preval with high treason for permitting U.N. troops to stay in Haiti.

Under Haiti's constitution, foreign troops are not allowed to occupy the country. U.N. peacekeepers have been patrolling since they replaced the 20,000 U.S. troops who restored former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power in 1994.

Aristide had been ousted in 1991 in a military coup. His home is now guarded by both U.N. troops and U.S. diplomatic security staff but he has recently made statements calling for a return to nationalism.
The U.N. troops are scheduled to pull out at the end of this month, but at Preval's request the Security Council will consider extending the mandate until Nov. 30.
"On July 31, the U.N. mission in Haiti should leave the country or else we will have to throw them out," Vanes Cherestal, a representative of the popular groups, said.
Graffitti saying the white soldiers must leave Haiti has been scrawled on walls throughout the capital in recent weeks.
